cards.explanation: The answer is the day of his birth. Job cursed the day he was born (Job 3:1). His wife had told him to curse God and die (Job 2:9), but his words land on a day on the calendar instead. I think there's a lot of pain packed into that choice, friends. Hold on to that, because it matters as we keep going.

The answer is disregard it. Job says, “May God above disregard it…” (Job 3:4). He wants that day treated like it was never worth a look. Then he adds that no light should shine on it, friends. That's a man who wants the whole day skipped over.

The answer is True. Job says it right out: “If only that day had turned to darkness!” (Job 3:4). He keeps going and asks that no light shine upon it. When Job wishes something away, he does it with the lights off.

The answer is that he had never been born. Job asks that the night “…not appear among the days of the year…” and that it never be entered in any of the months (Job 3:6). I think that's what's underneath all this: Job wishes his life had never started. It's a heavy thing to hear, friends.
The answer is False. Job asks, “Behold, may that night be barren; may no joyful voice come into it.” (Job 3:7). He's asking for no joyful voice in it, not a crowd of them.

The answer is daylight. Job says, “may it wait in vain for daylight; may it not see the breaking of dawn.” (Job 3:9). He wants that night to stay stuck in the dark with the sun never showing up. Picture waiting on a delivery that never comes, except it's a whole sunrise.

The answer is that it let him be born to see sorrow. Job gives his reason in Job 3:10: “For that night did not shut the doors of the womb to hide the sorrow from my eyes.” He's saying that night let him come into the world and see sorrow. Notice he says the sorrow itself, friends. He doesn't blame the night for anything else.

The answer is peace and rest. Job says, “For now I would be lying down in peace; I would be asleep and at rest” (Job 3:13). Peace and rest are what he's longing for. After all he's been through, I bet rest sounds like the most beautiful word on earth, friends.

The answer is kings and counselors. Job pictures himself resting “…with kings and counselors of the earth…” (Job 3:14). These are the people with big titles and big plans. He sees himself lying beside them, with nothing left to do. I think that's a quiet kind of equal.

The answer is False. Job describes kings and counselors “…who built for themselves cities now in ruins…” (Job 3:14). They built big, and now the cities are ruins. Job's point is that even these great builders are at rest.

The answer is True. Job says, “There the wicked cease from raging, and there the weary find rest.” (Job 3:17). Both halves are in the same verse. The wicked stop raging, and the weary finally get to rest. I think Job is leaning hard on that second part, friends.

The answer is False. Job says, “The captives enjoy their ease; they do not hear the voice of the oppressor.” (Job 3:18). The captives are at ease, and the oppressor's voice doesn't reach them. Job says they do not hear it, friends.

The answer is freed. Job says, “Both small and great are there, and the slave is freed from his master.” (Job 3:19). Small and great are both there, and the slave is freed from his master. Freed is the word Job uses, friends.

The answer is glad and full of joy. Job says these people “…rejoice and greatly exult when they reach the grave?” (Job 3:22). They had been searching for death like hidden treasure, and when they reach it, they're glad. This part is heavy, friends. I think it shows how deep their misery went.

The answer is sighs. Job says, “I sigh when food is put before me…” (Job 3:24). A plate of food is usually good news, and Job sighs at it. I think that tells you how heavy his days have gotten, friends.
The answer is False. Job says, “For the thing I feared has overtaken me, and what I dreaded has befallen me.” (Job 3:25). The trouble he was afraid of has arrived. It's not hiding anywhere, friends.
